title: Input shift versus a changed relationship
notes: CORE · 2 min explanation. Teaching purpose: First specify whether inputs changed or the target relationship changed. Mechanism and worked reasoning: Experiment B has an input-scale stress sweep and a separate coefficient reversal. Model parameters, evaluation procedure and the relevant paired rows stay fixed. Expected explanation: Changing inputs and labels together without controls makes the mechanism ambiguous. Separate interventions let us explain what each comparison can and cannot establish. title: Input shift changes which cases appear
notes: CORE · 3 min explanation. Teaching purpose: Change p(X) while retaining the same y=2x0+x1²+epsilon rule. Mechanism and worked reasoning: Generate 150 base rows once, keep x0,x2 and noise fixed, multiply x1 by 1, 1.5, 2.5 and recompute labels from the same rule. Do not refit or reselect either model. Ask: Does a wider Gaussian create new mathematical support? Expected explanation: No. Both normal distributions have unbounded support. The probability mass and observed range change; the training sample may sparsely cover the newly common regions. Visual interpretation: Analytic input distributions; only x1 scale changes in the paired stress test. Facilitation: get a prediction first, inspect matching notebook outputs, and distinguish finite empirical observations from population formulas. Live laboratory blocks include discussion and navigation through reference pages; do not time every page again. title: Pairing removes an avoidable comparison noise
notes: CORE · 3 min explanation. Teaching purpose: Use the same base observations and noise draws across stress conditions. Mechanism and worked reasoning: The intervention is x1 scale only. Ask: Why not redraw every condition independently? Expected explanation: An independent redraw changes both the stress condition and the random sample. A paired design makes the declared intervention easier to isolate in a small classroom experiment. Visual interpretation: Instructional protocol: highlighted dependency 1. title: Stress results depend on the fitted function
notes: CORE · 3 min explanation. Teaching purpose: A correct mean shape can respond differently from an affine approximation. Mechanism and worked reasoning: Plot frozen-model MAE against the three predeclared input scales. Compare the observed direction and magnitude with your prior prediction. The missing square becomes relevant where x1² is large. Ask: Must all models worsen under every input shift? Expected explanation: No. Risk depends on which regions gain probability, the conditional error there and finite sampling. Input change alone does not determine whether average performance improves or worsens. Visual interpretation: Actual notebook stress results on 150 paired synthetic rows. No refitting or reselection. Facilitation: get a prediction first, inspect matching notebook outputs, and distinguish finite empirical observations from population formulas. title: Concept change can hide behind stable inputs
notes: CORE · 4 min explanation. Teaching purpose: Keep the exact same X and noise; reverse the x0 coefficient from+2 to−2. Mechanism and worked reasoning: Frozen predictions do not change. New labels differ by−4x0, so the new residual equals the old residual+4x0. A stable input histogram therefore cannot certify stable predictive accuracy. Ask: Which monitoring signal is missing without labels? Expected explanation: Input monitoring alone cannot directly measure current prediction error or confirm the changed relationship. Delayed labels, residual patterns and domain evidence are needed. Visual interpretation: Declared coefficient reversal, paired noise and frozen models. Final panel uses actual notebook scores. Facilitation: get a prediction first, inspect matching notebook outputs, and distinguish finite empirical observations from population formulas. title: Monitoring is a diagnosis pipeline
notes: CORE · 3 min explanation. Teaching purpose: Detecting a change is different from knowing its cause or choosing a remedy. Mechanism and worked reasoning: Check input schema and units, input distributions, label timing and error slices. Inspect whether changes exceed expected variability, then investigate causes. Refit only with an explicit, reevaluated protocol. Ask: Is automatic retraining always an adequate response? Expected explanation: No. A unit bug, missing label or changed objective needs a different response. Retraining on corrupted or unrepresentative data can preserve the problem. Visual interpretation: Instructional protocol: highlighted dependency 1. No empirical performance claim. Facilitation: get a prediction first, inspect matching notebook outputs, and distinguish finite empirical observations from population formulas. Live laboratory blocks include discussion and navigation through reference pages; do not time every page again. title: An average changes with the case mixture
notes: REFERENCE · use during practice / no extra lecture time. Teaching purpose: Overall MAE is the weighted sum of group MAEs. Mechanism and worked reasoning: With losses 1 and 10, MAE=(1−q)×1+q×10. At q=.10 it is 1.9; at q=.25 it is 3.25. Both within-group losses can stay fixed while the aggregate changes. Ask: What should accompany an overall score? Expected explanation: Group definitions, counts and within-group losses, together with units and evaluation conditions. Do not substitute the illustrative90/10 mixture for the actual test group counts. Visual interpretation: Paper illustration: fixed group losses 1 and 10. These are not fitted-model test scores. Facilitation: get a prediction first, inspect matching notebook outputs, and distinguish finite empirical observations from population formulas. Live laboratory blocks include discussion and navigation through reference pages; do not time every page again.
